notes.text: Tamil writes one letter for k and g. Between vowels it softens by itself, so pakal is heard as pagal.
Vanakkam grew from vanangu, to bow. One word covers morning, noon and midnight; Tamil never swapped greetings by the clock.
Tamil has two words for we. Naanga leaves you out, naama includes you. Choosing wrongly can sound cold to new friends.
Tamil ranks siblings before it names them: anna is older brother, thambi younger. There is no neutral word for brother.
Two kinds of hot: sudu is temperature, kaaram is chilli. Coffee is sudu, sambar is kaaram, and never the reverse.
Spoken Tamil trims its numbers. Onru becomes onnu, irandu becomes rendu. Learn both, or the shopkeeper will lose you.
Pachai means green and raw at once: pachai milagai is a green chilli, pachai thanni is plain uncooked water.
Strangers on a bus will ask ungal ooru enna. Ooru is not any town, it is the one your family belongs to.
Tamil months sit across English ones. Chithirai runs mid April to mid May and opens the Tamil year.
Add nga to any order and it turns polite. Vaa becomes vaanga, kudu becomes kudunga. Bargain with it and shopkeepers soften.
Tamil rarely says I am ill. You say udambu sari illa, the body is not right, keeping the sickness at arm's length.
Veedu means house today, but in old Tamil poetry it meant release, the final freedom. Going home was the same word.
Nobody at work calls an elder by name alone. You say Kumar anna or Priya akka, name first, respect after.
English love splits three ways here: kadhal for lovers, anbu for kindness, paasam for the pull of family. Pick carefully.
Pongal is a verb before a festival: to boil over. When the milk rises, everyone shouts Pongalo Pongal at the pot.
